etymology: From tale, a report or story, and bearer, one who carries; hence one who carries reports from house to house. It renders the Hebrew rakil, from the root rakal, “to go about as a trader or pedlar” — the talebearer is a merchant, and his wares are his neighbour’s secrets.
biblical_def: A talebearer is one who traffics in the private matters of other men, gathering in one house what he will peddle in the next. The Hebrew names the trade exactly: rakil is kin to the travelling merchant, and the talebearer goes up and down with his pack of secrets, dealing them out where they will fetch the best attention. The law forbids the trade outright: “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:16). Mark the company the sin keeps — talebearing is set in the same breath with standing against a neighbour’s blood, for the tongue that peddles tales is a slow murderer, and the LORD signs the prohibition with His own name. Solomon anatomizes it. “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter” (Pro 11:13): the mark of a faithful man is a shut mouth, and the mark of the talebearer is that nothing entrusted to him stays entrusted. “The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly” (Pro 18:8) — they are swallowed like dainty morsels and lodge where no argument can afterward reach them; a tale once heard is never wholly unheard. And the remedy is starvation, not debate: “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth” (Pro 26:20). Strife is a fire, and the talebearer is the man with the armload of kindling.
webster_summary: One who officiously carries tales; a pedlar of his neighbour’s secrets, who tells private matters abroad and makes mischief thereby.
webster_full: TALEBEARER, a person who officiously tells tales; one who impertinently communicates intelligence or anecdotes, and makes mischief by his officiousness.
From tale, a report or story, and bearer, one who carries a thing from place to place.
The Hebrew rakil is kin to the pedlar: the talebearer trades in secrets as a merchant trades in wares.
The law forbids a man to go up and down as a talebearer among his people (Lev 19:16).
His words are as wounds that sink into the belly, and where he is absent the strife ceaseth (Pro 18:8; Pro 26:20).
scriptures: Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD.
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.
Pro 18:8
The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
corruption_summary: Live and thriving: the age has not abolished the talebearer but rebranded him — the tale is now carried in as a concern, a caution, or a prayer request.
corruption_paragraphs: No man calls himself a talebearer. He calls himself informed, or burdened, or merely honest; and the tale is brought in under cover of a kindness. “I only tell you so that you may pray.” “I am simply sharing a concern.” “You ought to know what she is really like.” The preface is new; the sin is precisely what Moses forbade. To carry a matter to an ear that has no business with it is talebearing, though it be spoken in a hushed voice with a sorrowful face and closed with an amen. Our own generation has multiplied the trade beyond Solomon’s reckoning, for the pedlar now needs no feet: a matter whispered in a house at noon is peddled to a thousand ears by nightfall, and the wares never spoil. The LORD who wrote His name at the end of Lev 19:16 has not repealed it because the pack is lighter to carry.

The principle to recover is twofold, and both halves are in Proverbs. First, be the man of a faithful spirit who concealeth the matter (Pro 11:13) — not the man who hides sin, for Christ commands that a brother who trespasses be gone to and told his fault between thee and him alone, but the man in whose keeping a confidence is safe, who will not sell his neighbour’s shame for the price of an interested face. Second, starve the fire. “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out.” The talebearer cannot peddle what no one will buy, and the man who refuses to be the ear does as much for the peace of the church as the man who refuses to be the mouth. Stop receiving the wares and the trade fails.
roots_summary: The word means one who carries tales — a pedlar of other men’s secrets.
roots_lines: Talebearer — from tale, a report, and bearer, one who carries.

Where no wood is, the fire goeth out: refuse to be the ear, and the talebearer’s trade fails.

etymology: From whisper, Old English hwisprian, “to speak with a low sibilant breath” — a word formed from the very sound it names. It renders the Greek psithuristēs (from psithurizo, to whisper), the man who works in the ear, and the Hebrew nirgan, the murmurer.
biblical_def: A whisperer is the secret sower of division — not the man who rails aloud, but the man who leans to the ear. Scripture keeps him distinct from the backbiter: the backbiter speaks against a man openly and in his absence, but the whisperer works under his breath, dropping a hint here and a question there, never quite saying the thing he means to plant. Solomon marks his work by its fruit: “A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends” (Pro 16:28). Chief friends — not strangers, but men bound to one another — are prised apart by a tongue too soft to be answered, for a whisper can be denied where a charge must be proved. Beside it stands the twin proverb: “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends” (Pro 17:9). Love covers; the whisperer repeats. Paul sets whisperers in the black catalogue of the reprobate mind, given over of God (Rom 1:29) — the whisper is listed with murder and malignity, for God does not grade sins by their volume. And he fears to find whisperings among the Corinthian saints (2Co 12:20): it is a church-destroying sin, needing no pulpit, no majority, and no evidence, but only a quiet corner and a willing ear. David knew the sound of it from beneath: “All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt” (Psa 41:7) — and that psalm, whose familiar friend lifted up his heel, our Lord took upon His own lips of Judas. Christ Himself was whispered about, and betrayed under a man’s breath.
webster_summary: One who tells secrets under his breath; a secret sower of division, who separates friends by hints and half-said things.
webster_full: WHISPERER, one who whispers; one who tells secrets; a backbiter under his breath.
From Old English hwisprian, a word formed from the sibilant sound it names.
The Greek psithuristēs denotes the man who works secretly in the ear, distinct from the open evil-speaker.
A whisperer separateth chief friends, and he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends (Pro 16:28; Pro 17:9).
Paul numbers whisperers with the reprobate (Rom 1:29) and fears whisperings among the saints (2Co 12:20).
scriptures: A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends.
Pro 17:9
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
Rom 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
Psa 41:7

corruption_summary: Wholly live: ours is a whispering age, and it has learned to call the whisper discernment, transparency, or the raising of a question.
corruption_paragraphs: The whisperer thrives because he can never be pinned. He does not accuse; he wonders aloud. He does not charge; he asks whether anyone else has noticed. He does not testify against an elder before two or three witnesses, as Paul requires; he lets a doubt loose in a corner and lets other men carry it. The age has given him a whole vocabulary of respectable names — he is only being transparent, only exercising discernment, only asking the hard question — and by these he does in a fortnight what an open accuser could not do in a year, because a whisper cannot be answered. There is no defence against a thing never plainly said. This is precisely why Scripture will not let the sin hide behind its volume: Paul lists the whisperer with the murderer in Rom 1:29, and God does not grade sins by their loudness.

The principle to recover is that love covers and the whisperer repeats. “He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.” Covering is not conniving at sin — Christ commands that a sinning brother be told his fault, and Paul commands that a charge against an elder be brought before witnesses. Covering means that where a matter can be borne in silence it is borne, and where it must be spoken it is spoken to the man’s face and not behind his back. The whisper does the opposite of both: it neither covers nor confronts. It separates chief friends and leaves the whisperer’s hands clean. Let the saints resolve to say to the whisperer’s face what he would say in their ear, and the whispering ends.
roots_summary: The word means one who whispers — the secret sower of division who works in the ear.

etymology: From back and bite — one who bites at the back, who tears at a man where he cannot see nor defend himself, as a cur snaps at the heel of a passer-by. It renders the Greek katalalos, “a speaker-against,” and the Hebrew ragal, “to go about on foot” as a spy or slanderer.
biblical_def: A backbiter is one who speaks evil of a man behind his back — who tears at his name where he cannot answer, as a dog bites the heel of one already gone by; the wound is in the back, and the bite is real. Where the whisperer works secretly in the ear, the backbiter speaks out; the Greek katalalos is simply a speaker-against, an open evil-speaker who wants no cover but the absence of his victim. David sets the sin at the door of God’s house: asking who shall abide in the LORD’s tabernacle, he answers, “He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour” (Psa 15:3) — and taking up a reproach is condemned with the making of it. He who repeats an evil report is a backbiter though the tale be none of his coining. Solomon prescribes the remedy: “The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue” (Pro 25:23). A cold look scatters the evil-speaker as the north wind scatters the clouds; he speaks because he is welcomed, and a face that refuses to be entertained will shut his mouth faster than an argument. Paul places backbiters in the roll of the reprobate mind, hard by the haters of God (Rom 1:30). And David, setting the rule of his own house, will not have such a man about him at all: “Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer” (Psa 101:5). The bite is no less a wound because the wounded man never sees the teeth.
webster_summary: One who speaks evil of an absent man; a secret calumniator, who tears at a name behind its owner’s back.
webster_full: BACKBITER, a secret calumniator; one who censures or reproaches an absent person.
From back and bite: the wound is given where a man cannot see nor defend himself.
It renders the Greek katalalos, a speaker-against — the open evil-speaker, as distinct from the whisperer.
He that backbiteth not is marked among the dwellers in God’s tabernacle (Psa 15:3).
An angry countenance drives away a backbiting tongue as the north wind drives away rain (Pro 25:23).
scriptures: Psa 15:3
He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour.
The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.
Rom 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,
Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.
corruption_summary: Live: the age keeps the bite and drops the name, calling it candour, venting, or telling it like it is — and it counts the hearer innocent.
corruption_paragraphs: Backbiting has kept every one of its teeth and lost only its ugly name. It is now candour, or venting, or refusing to pretend, or simply telling it like it is; and a generation that would be scandalized to be called a slanderer will spend an hour tearing at a brother’s reputation and call it honesty. But honesty is not the question. A thing may be true and still be a bite, if it is spoken where the man cannot answer and to hearers who cannot help. That is why Psa 15:3 does not ask whether the report is accurate: it asks whether thou hast taken up a reproach against thy neighbour. Paul’s catalogue is more sobering still. Backbiters stand in Rom 1:30 next to haters of God and inventors of evil things — not because a sharp word equals blasphemy in its measure, but because the tongue that will not spare a brother has learned its appetite in the same fallen heart.

The principle to recover is that the ear is as guilty as the mouth, and the cure is in the face. David condemns him that taketh up a reproach as well as him that makes it; the man who forwards the evil report has bitten his neighbour with borrowed teeth. And Solomon does not tell us to argue the backbiter down — he tells us to look at him: “The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.” The evil-speaker speaks because he is entertained. A grave face, an unamused silence, a plain word that this man is not here to answer for himself, and the clouds scatter. The saints who mean to have peace in the church will not answer backbiting with backbiting; they will simply decline to be its weather.
roots_summary: The word means one who bites at the back — who speaks evil of an absent man.

It renders the Greek katalalos, “a speaker-against,” the open evil-speaker.
He is barred from the tabernacle of the LORD (Psa 15:3).
An angry countenance drives him away as the north wind drives rain (Pro 25:23).
usage: He that backbiteth not with his tongue shall abide in the tabernacle of the LORD.
To take up a reproach is to bite with borrowed teeth — the hearer is no innocent.
As the north wind driveth away rain, so an angry countenance shuts a backbiting tongue.

etymology: Strange, from Old French estrange and Latin extraneus, “from without, foreign, belonging to another.” It renders the Hebrew zarah and nokriyyah — the woman who is another man’s, or no man’s: not strange as in odd, but strange as in not thine.
biblical_def: The strange woman of Proverbs is not the eccentric woman but the woman who is not thine — the adulteress, the harlot, the wife of another, the outsider to the covenant of thy marriage. The Hebrew words mean foreign, belonging elsewhere; and the whole warning of Proverbs 2 and 5 and 7 turns upon that one point. She is not yours, and every delight she promises is stolen. Wisdom’s first office is deliverance from her: she comes “to deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words” (Pro 2:16), and again the father charges his son to keep wisdom “that they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words” (Pro 7:5). Twice the weapon named is flattery, not force. She does not overpower the young man void of understanding; she tells him what he wishes were true. “For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil” (Pro 5:3) — honey on the lip and oil in the mouth, and then wormwood and a two-edged sword at the end, her feet going down to death. Solomon closes the account with the plainest of warnings: “The mouth of strange women is a deep pit: he that is abhorred of the LORD shall fall therein” (Pro 22:14). A pit is not argued with; it is avoided. And the whole of it is set against the fountain of one’s own: rejoice with the wife of thy youth, and be thou ravished always with her love.
webster_summary: In Proverbs, the adulteress or harlot — the woman who belongs to another or to none; strange not as odd but as not thine own.
webster_full: STRANGE, foreign; belonging to another country, another family, or another person; not one’s own.
From Latin extraneus, “from without”; the strange woman is the woman who is not thine.
It renders the Hebrew zarah and nokriyyah, the outsider to the marriage covenant.
Her weapon is flattery: she flattereth with her words (Pro 2:16; Pro 7:5).
Her lips drop as an honeycomb, but her end is bitter as wormwood, and her mouth is a deep pit (Pro 5:3; Pro 22:14).
scriptures: Pro 2:16
To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words;
Pro 5:3
For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil:
Pro 7:5
That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words.

corruption_summary: Wholly live: the sexual revolution has taken the honeycomb and hidden the wormwood, and it flatters exactly as Solomon said she would.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon named the weapon three thousand years before the sexual revolution picked it up: she flattereth. Not compels — flatters. And the sixty years since the pill and the Playboy philosophy have been one long campaign of flattery, telling the young man and the young woman precisely what the fallen heart wishes were true: that desire is its own warrant, that the body may be spent without spending the soul, that fidelity is a cage and the covenant a formality, that no one is hurt and nothing is owed. Every one of those is a lie with honey on it. Solomon does not deny that her lips are sweet — he says they drop as an honeycomb, and he says her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword, and her feet go down to death. The revolution has kept the honeycomb in the advertisement and left the wormwood out of the fine print, and a generation of broken homes, fatherless children, and used-up hearts is the bill coming due.

The principle to recover is that Scripture’s remedy is not vigilance at the edge of the pit but distance from it. “The mouth of strange women is a deep pit” — and no man argues with a pit; he keeps off the ground. Wisdom is called to deliver, and the father’s counsel is to remove thy way far from her and come not nigh the door of her house. Let it be said plainly that Proverbs addresses the son and warns him of the adulteress, but Scripture is not one-eyed: the same law that condemns her condemns him, whoremongers and adulterers God will judge, and the man who plays the strange woman’s part is under the same sentence. The positive command is sweeter than the prohibition: drink waters out of thine own cistern, let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth — for the cure for a stolen honeycomb is a lawful one.

etymology: Brawl, to quarrel noisily, to wrangle; of uncertain Middle English origin, perhaps imitative of the noise. It renders the Hebrew midyanim, “contentions, strivings” — literally a woman of contentions, whose element is the quarrel.
biblical_def: The brawling woman of Proverbs is the contentious wife — the woman whose element is the quarrel, who wrangles as a matter of habit and makes a wide house a narrow place. The Hebrew does not say she brawls occasionally; it calls her a woman of contentions, as another might be called a man of war. Solomon returns to her four times, and twice in the same words, as though the proverb itself were a continual dropping. “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house” (Pro 21:9; and again Pro 25:24) — the flat roof, exposed to sun and rain, with room for one man to lie down, is preferred to a mansion with a quarrel in it. He goes further: “It is better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman” (Pro 21:19). Better the wilderness, with its beasts and its thirst, than a home at war. And he names the peculiar torment of it: “A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike” (Pro 27:15). It is not the thunderclap but the drip — no single drop worth complaining of, and no hour without one, until the roof itself gives way. The sin is not that she speaks; the Proverbs 31 woman openeth her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness. The sin is that she strives, and strives, and will not have peace.
webster_summary: The contentious wife of Proverbs — a woman of quarrels, whose continual striving makes a wide house a narrow one.
webster_full: BRAWLING, quarrelsome; given to noisy contention and wrangling.
It renders the Hebrew midyanim, “contentions” — a woman of contentions, as a man may be called a man of war.
Better a corner of the housetop than a wide house with her in it (Pro 21:9; Pro 25:24).
Better the wilderness than a contentious and an angry woman (Pro 21:19).
She is likened to a continual dropping in a very rainy day (Pro 27:15).
scriptures: Pro 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.
As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
corruption_summary: Live: the age has made contention in the home a virtue and submission a shame — but Scripture rebukes the contentious man just as sharply as the brawling woman.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not of the word but of the home. Our age has taught a generation of wives that contention is strength, that the quarrel is how a woman keeps her selfhood, and that to yield anything to a husband is to lose something of herself — and it has taught them to hear Eph 5:22-33 and 1Pe 3:1-7 as an insult to be explained away rather than as the Word of the God who made them. But God ordered the home before the fall and not because of it: the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, and the wife’s ordered submission is no more a shame to her than the Son’s to the Father is a shame to Him. Peter praises the meek and quiet spirit as an ornament of great price — not silence, not weakness, but a soul at rest and therefore not at war. The brawling woman has not gained an inch of ground by her striving; Solomon says she has only driven her husband to the roof.

Two things must be said plainly, or the proverb will be made a club. First, the honour of the woman herself: Scripture’s picture of a wife is the Proverbs 31 woman, who buys a field and plants a vineyard and stretches out her hand to the poor and laughs at the time to come, who openeth her mouth with wisdom, and in whose tongue is the law of kindness — a strong, working, speaking, honoured woman whose husband praiseth her in the gates. The rebuke is not to her strength; it is to contention. Second, the men. The same Solomon writes, “As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife” (Pro 26:21), and Paul commands the husband to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, and forbids him to be bitter against her. A husband who is himself the coals and blames the fire has read Proverbs with one eye. The house is to be at peace, and both who dwell in it are commanded to keep it so.
roots_summary: The phrase means a woman of contentions — the quarrelsome wife whose striving makes a wide house narrow.

Her likeness is the continual dropping of a very rainy day (Pro 27:15).
usage: Better a corner of the housetop than a wide house with a brawling woman in it.
A continual dropping and a contentious woman are alike — it is the drip, not the thunder, that wears the roof through.
The rebuke is to contention, not to strength: the Proverbs 31 woman openeth her mouth with wisdom.

etymology: From sloth, Middle English slouthe, from Old English slaw, “slow” — slowness made a habit and then a character. It renders the Hebrew atsel, the sluggard, and the Greek oknēros, shrinking, hesitating, loth to move.
biblical_def: Slothful means slow — but slow settled into the bones until it is no longer a pace but a person. Scripture never treats sloth as a temperament to be indulged; it treats it as a sin to be repented of, and it mocks it. Solomon sends the sluggard to school under an insect: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Pro 6:6). The ant has no guide, overseer, or ruler, and yet provideth her meat in the summer; the sluggard has reason, a conscience, and a Bible, and provideth nothing. Then comes the question that has awakened more men than a trumpet: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?” (Pro 6:9) — and the answer is that yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep, and poverty comes as one that travelleth. Proverbs 26 is a whole portrait: he cries there is a lion in the way, inventing perils to excuse inaction; he turns upon his bed as the door upon its hinges, all motion and no progress; he hides his hand in his bosom and it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth. And the last stroke is the cruellest: “The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason” (Pro 26:16). Sloth is not humble; it is proud, and it always has an explanation. Our Lord seals the matter at the judgment: “Thou wicked and slothful servant” (Mat 25:26) — wicked and slothful, joined with an and that no man may put asunder.
webster_summary: Slow; sluggish; inactive; indisposed to labour — slowness hardened into a habit and a character.
webster_full: SLOTHFUL, inactive; sluggish; lazy; indolent; idle; averse to labour or exertion.
From Old English slaw, “slow”: the word is slowness made a settled habit.
It renders the Hebrew atsel, the sluggard, and the Greek oknēros, shrinking or loth to move.
The sluggard is sent to the ant for instruction and found wiser in his own conceit than seven wise men (Pro 6:6; Pro 26:16).
The Lord calls the unprofitable servant wicked and slothful in one breath (Mat 25:26).

Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
His lord answered and said unto him, Thou wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed:
corruption_summary: Live: sloth is the one deadly sin the age has agreed to excuse, renaming it burnout, low capacity, or a season of rest — while Christ still calls it wicked.
corruption_paragraphs: Of the old catalogue of deadly sins, sloth is the one our generation has quietly struck from the list. Pride we still resent in other men; greed we still prosecute; but sloth we have renamed and pensioned off. It is burnout now, or low capacity, or a season, or simply not where I am right now — and the sluggard is not called to repent but offered a diagnosis. Understand what is being lost. Scripture knows real weakness and real weariness: Elijah under the juniper was fed and let sleep, the Lord Himself slept in the ship, and He is a merciful High Priest who knoweth our frame and remembereth that we are dust. There is a rest God commands and a bed God gives His beloved. But there is also a man who hides his hand in his bosom because it grieveth him to lift it to his own mouth, and Scripture does not offer him a category. It offers him an ant.

The principle to recover is that sloth is not a temperament but a transgression, and that it is proud. Note what Proverbs actually mocks: not the sluggard’s slowness only, but his reasons. He has a lion in the street. He turns on his hinges and calls it motion. And he is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason — which is to say he can always out-argue anyone who tells him to get up. That is the real disease: sloth is a sin that comes with its own defence attorney. Christ strips the defence away in one word at the judgment. The man who buried his talent had an explanation ready, and a good one, and the Lord answered it with, “Thou wicked and slothful servant.” Whatever mercy the weary may claim, and they may claim much, no man may claim the excuse the Lord Himself refused to accept.
roots_summary: The word means slow, sluggish, averse to labour — slowness hardened into a character.
roots_lines: Slothful — from Old English slaw, “slow,” through Middle English slouthe.
It renders the Hebrew atsel, the sluggard, and the Greek oknēros, loth to move.
The sluggard’s tutor is the ant, who has no overseer and yet provideth her meat (Pro 6:6).
His besetting mark is a ready excuse: a lion in the way, and wisdom in his own conceit (Pro 26:16).
Christ joins the words: “Thou wicked and slothful servant” (Mat 25:26).
usage: Go to the ant, thou sluggard: she has no overseer and provideth her meat; thou hast a Bible and providest nothing.
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? — a question that has waked more men than a trumpet.
Wicked and slothful: Christ joined the words, and no excuse may put them asunder.

etymology: From naughty, Middle English naughty, “having naught, worth nothing,” from naught (Old English nawiht, “no thing”). A naughty man is a man of naught — a moral nothing. It renders the Hebrew havvah, mischief and calamity, roa', evil, and the Greek kakia, malice or wickedness.
biblical_def: Naughtiness in the KJV is not mischief; it is wickedness. The word is built on naught — nothing — and a naughty man is a man of naught, a worthless man, one whose moral substance amounts to nil. Solomon uses it of the ruin a man’s own evil brings on him: “The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness” (Pro 11:6). Taken — caught as in a snare of their own setting; the wickedness a man weaves is the net he is carried off in. He uses it of the tongue: “A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue” (Pro 17:4), where the naughty tongue is the mischief-making, ruinous tongue, and the ear that welcomes it is already condemned. Eliab flings the word at David before Goliath: “I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart” (1Sa 17:28) — no man charges his brother with childish antics in front of an army; Eliab is calling David wicked to the core, and the charge is false, which is precisely why it is so bitter. And James makes the word carry the whole weight of indwelling sin: “lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21). The superfluity of naughtiness is the overflowing surplus of wickedness in the heart, the rank growth that must be stripped away before the engrafted word can take.
webster_summary: In the old and biblical sense, wickedness; moral worthlessness — from naught, nothing: the naughty man is a man of naught.
webster_full: NAUGHTINESS, badness; wickedness of heart or life; the quality of being worth naught.
NAUGHTY, bad; wicked; corrupt; worthless. From naught, nothing — a man of naught.
It renders the Hebrew havvah (mischief, calamity) and roa' (evil), and the Greek kakia (malice).
Transgressors are taken in their own naughtiness, as in a snare of their own setting (Pro 11:6).
James bids us lay apart the superfluity of naughtiness — the rank surplus of wickedness in the heart (Jas 1:21).
scriptures: Pro 11:6
The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness.
Pro 17:4
A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue.

And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle.
Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
corruption_summary: A real and worthy corruption: a word that once meant wickedness now means a toddler’s mischief or a wink at vice — and the softening has cost us the doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption worth naming, because it happened quietly and nobody objected. Naughty once meant worth naught — morally nothing, a man of no substance, wicked. That is its force in every KJV verse. Today it means one of two things, and neither is the old sense: a small child who has drawn on the wall, or a coy euphemism for vice, the wink that turns lewdness into a joke. The one use makes wickedness cute; the other makes it flirtatious. Between them they have emptied a strong word of everything it carried. And the loss is not merely lexical. Read Jas 1:21 with the modern sense and it becomes an apostle asking grown men to stop being a bit cheeky; read it with the old sense and it is what it is — a command to strip off the rank, overflowing wickedness of the heart before the engrafted word can be received to the saving of the soul. A generation that has no strong word for wickedness will not long believe in it.

The principle to recover is the arithmetic in the root. Naught is nothing. Sin does not merely stain a man; it hollows him, so that the transgressor is a man of naught, and his righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and every imagination of the thoughts of his heart is only evil continually. That is the doctrine of total depravity spoken in one small Saxon word. And Solomon adds the justice of it: “transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness” — the net that catches the wicked is woven by the wicked. But mark where James lands. He does not say lay apart the superfluity of naughtiness and be better; he says lay it apart and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls. The man of naught cannot make himself something. He is stripped that Christ may be engrafted, and the worthless is made an heir.
roots_summary: The word means wickedness, moral worthlessness — from naught, nothing.
roots_lines: Naughtiness — from naughty, “having naught,” from Old English nawiht, “no thing.”
A naughty man is a man of naught: his moral substance amounts to nothing.
It renders the Hebrew havvah and roa', and the Greek kakia, malice.
Transgressors are taken in their own naughtiness, snared by their own weaving (Pro 11:6).
The superfluity of naughtiness must be laid apart for the engrafted word (Jas 1:21).
usage: Naughtiness in the KJV is wickedness, not mischief: the naughty man is a man of naught.
Transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness — the net is of their own weaving.
Lay apart the superfluity of naughtiness and receive the engrafted word, which is able to save.

etymology: From riot, Old French riote, “dispute, debauchery, wanton excess” — not chiefly a mob but a life of unrestrained indulgence. In Luk 15:13 it renders the Greek asōtōs, from a- (not) and sōzō (to save): living unsavingly, spending what cannot be recovered.
biblical_def: Riotous in the KJV rarely means a mob in the street; it means a life of unbridled excess — eating, drinking, and spending without restraint or reckoning. Solomon binds the riotous to the table: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh” (Pro 23:20), and gives the reason in the next breath — “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). The picture is not a moment of scandal but a slow undressing: the man who will not govern his appetite is clothed at last in rags, and it is his own drowsy indulgence that stripped him. The Greek behind the word is more terrible still. When the prodigal “wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luk 15:13), Luke uses asōtōs — literally unsavingly, from the same root as the word for salvation. He lived in a way that saves nothing and recovers nothing; every coin, every hour, every faculty went out and none came back. That is the essence of riot: not merely pleasure, but expenditure that cannot be reclaimed. Peter shows the other edge of it: the heathen “think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you” (1Pe 4:4) — riot resents the sober man’s refusal to run along. Paul forbids it to the church without qualification: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness” (Rom 13:13). Yet the prodigal’s far country ends in a swine-trough, and there he came to himself, and rose, and went to his father — and the father ran.
webster_summary: Given to unrestrained excess and dissipation; wasteful, luxurious, unbridled — living unsavingly, spending what cannot be recovered.
webster_full: RIOTOUS, luxurious; wanton; given to excess in feasting or dissipation; wasteful.
From Old French riote, “debauchery, wanton excess”; the mob-sense is later and secondary.
The Greek asōtōs is a- (not) + sōzō (to save): living unsavingly, keeping nothing back.
The riotous eater and the winebibber come to poverty, and drowsiness clothes them with rags (Pro 23:20-21).
The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living in a far country (Luk 15:13).
scriptures: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
corruption_summary: Live: the age has made riot a rite of passage and calls sober restraint a joyless thing — but riot is spending what can never be got back.
corruption_paragraphs: Our generation has made riot a rite of passage. The far country is now a stage of life to be got through rather than a sin to be fled, and the years a young man spends wasting his substance are indulged as experience, as finding himself, as something everyone does. Peter saw the mechanism plainly: the heathen think it strange that ye run not with them, and they speak evil of you. Riot is never content to be private; it wants company, and it punishes refusal with mockery, because the sober man’s existence is itself a rebuke. So the restraint Scripture commands is recast as joylessness, and the man who will not run is told he is missing his life. Solomon answers the mockery with an inventory: the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty, and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags. The far country always sends a bill, and it is always paid in the one currency a man cannot earn back.

The principle to recover is written in the Greek itself. Asōtōs is un-savingly — the prodigal lived in a manner that saved nothing. Not merely that he enjoyed himself, but that everything went out and nothing came back: his substance, his years, his strength, his father’s honour, all spent past recovery. That is the true horror of riot; it is not the pleasure but the irrecoverableness. And yet this word is set in the one parable where irrecoverableness meets grace. The son who could save nothing came to himself among the swine, and rose, and went to his father with a rehearsed speech about being no more worthy — and while he was yet a great way off his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. The prodigal could not recover what he had spent. His father recovered him. That is the gospel, and it is why riot is a sin to be repented of and never a life to be admired.
roots_summary: The word means given to unrestrained excess — living unsavingly, spending past recovery.
roots_lines: Riotous — from Old French riote, “dispute, debauchery, wanton excess.”
The mob-sense is later; the KJV sense is unbridled indulgence and waste.
In Luk 15:13 it renders the Greek asōtōs, a- (not) + sōzō (to save).
To live riotously is to live unsavingly: nothing kept, nothing recovered.
Its wages are poverty, and drowsiness clothes the man with rags (Pro 23:21).
usage: Be not among winebibbers, among riotous eaters of flesh: the table has undone more men than the sword.
The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living — living unsavingly, keeping nothing back.
They think it strange that ye run not with them: riot always resents the man who will not run.

etymology: From Middle English wantowen: wan-, a negative prefix (“lacking, un-”), and towen, “trained, disciplined, brought up” — hence undisciplined, unbroken, untrained. The wanton is not merely lustful but ungoverned.
biblical_def: Wanton means undisciplined. The Middle English is wan-towen, un-trained — the word for a colt never broken to the bridle — and every biblical use turns on that root. Isaiah names it in the eye: the daughters of Zion “are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isa 3:16). The Hebrew is the eye that ogles, that goes wandering after what it wants; the neck is stretched, the step is studied, the very ankles are made to ring — a whole body trained to be looked at and untrained to any other law. Paul uses the word of the heart’s revolt: the younger widows, he says, “when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry” (1Ti 5:11). Wanton against Christ — the Greek pictures the young beast kicking against the rein it once bore. Desire that will not be governed does not merely wander; it turns and strikes at the hand that holds it. And James lays the word on the rich oppressors in the day of judgment: “Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter” (Jas 5:5). Fattening the heart on pleasure while the sentence is being pronounced — that is wantonness at its ripest. Ezekiel sums the end of it in two words: “the lewd women” (Eze 23:44). Wantonness begins as a look and ends as an identity.
webster_summary: Undisciplined, unrestrained, ungoverned; hence lascivious, loose, and given to unbridled desire.
webster_full: WANTON, wandering or roving in gaiety; licentious; lascivious; unrestrained; not governed by law or moral restraint.
From Middle English wan-towen: wan-, un-, and towen, “trained, disciplined.” The wanton is the unbroken colt.
Isaiah names the wanton eye among the finery of the haughty daughters of Zion (Isa 3:16).
To wax wanton against Christ is to kick against the rein once borne (1Ti 5:11).
The wanton nourish their hearts as in a day of slaughter (Jas 5:5).
scriptures: Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
But the younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry;
Jas 5:5
Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter.
Yet they went in unto her, as they go in unto a woman that playeth the harlot: so went they in unto Aholah and unto Aholibah, the lewd women.
corruption_summary: Live: the age has made ungovernedness the definition of freedom, and it begins where Isaiah said it begins — in the eye.
corruption_paragraphs: Take the etymology seriously and the modern corruption stands exposed. Wanton is un-trained; and our generation has decided that to be untrained is to be free. Discipline is repression, restraint is shame, and the governed appetite is a life half-lived — so runs the creed. But Scripture says the unbroken colt is not free; it is merely useless, and eventually it is dangerous. Paul’s phrase is the one to sit with: to wax wanton against Christ. Ungoverned desire is not neutral. It does not simply wander off; it turns and kicks at the Lord who holds the rein, because a desire that will bow to nothing has already made itself a god and cannot abide a rival. The man who says he answers to no law has not escaped a master; he has only exchanged the Lord of glory for the most tyrannical master a soul can serve, which is itself.

The principle to recover is that Isaiah locates the whole disease in the eye. Before the mincing and the tinkling, before Aholah and Aholibah, there is the wanton eye — the look that goes roving after what it wants and the look that is arranged to be wanted. Both are in Isa 3:16, and both are still with us; only the ornaments have changed, and the tinkling now travels at the speed of light and into every pocket. So Job made a covenant with his eyes, and Christ said that whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart, and John warned of the lust of the eyes as one of the three things not of the Father but of the world. The cure is not a stricter watch on behaviour but a broken and bridled heart: put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
roots_summary: The word means undisciplined, ungoverned — hence lascivious and unrestrained.
roots_lines: Wanton — Middle English wantowen: wan- (un-) + towen (trained).
The root picture is a colt never broken to the bridle: undisciplined, not merely lustful.
Isaiah names the wanton eye — the eye that roves and the eye arranged to be seen (Isa 3:16).
To wax wanton against Christ is to kick against the rein once borne (1Ti 5:11).
Its end is a day of slaughter with a heart fattened on pleasure (Jas 5:5).
usage: Wanton is un-trained: the wanton is the colt that was never broken to the bridle.
The daughters of Zion walked with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes — a body trained to be looked at.
To wax wanton against Christ is not to wander from the rein but to kick at the hand that holds it.

etymology: From the Latin rudis, “raw, unwrought, rough” — said of stone not yet dressed or timber not yet planed; hence unpolished, untrained, lacking finish. In 2Co 11:6 it renders the Greek idiōtēs, a private man, a layman, one not professionally skilled.
biblical_def: Rude in the KJV does not mean discourteous. The Latin rudis is said of a block of stone not yet dressed or a beam not yet planed: rude is unfinished, raw, unpolished, without the trained gloss of the schools. It appears once, and gloriously, when Paul answers the Corinthians who preferred the smooth professional orators: “But though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge; but we have been throughly made manifest among you in all things” (2Co 11:6). His accusers had said his letters were weighty but his bodily presence weak and his speech contemptible; he does not deny the charge, he concedes it and moves the ground. Grant that the polish is not there. The knowledge is. The Greek is idiōtēs — a layman, a man without the guild’s training — the very word Luke uses of Peter and John, whom the council perceived to be “unlearned and ignorant men,” and marvelled, “and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13). And it is Paul’s deliberate method, not merely his limitation: “I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God” (1Co 2:1); “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4). Rude speech and a risen Christ turned the world over. The polish was in Corinth; the power was in the plain word of the cross.
webster_summary: Raw, unwrought, unpolished, untaught — in Paul, unskilled in the orator’s art, not discourteous.
webster_full: RUDE, rough; uneven; unformed by art; artless; untaught; ignorant of the polite arts.
From the Latin rudis, said of stone undressed or timber unplaned: the word means unfinished.
The modern sense of discourteous is a later narrowing; it is not the KJV’s sense.
It renders the Greek idiōtēs, a private man or layman without professional training (2Co 11:6).
The same word describes Peter and John, unlearned men who had been with Jesus (Act 4:13).
scriptures: But though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge; but we have been throughly made manifest among you in all things.
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
corruption_summary: A word narrowed almost to nothing: rude once meant unpolished, and reading “rude in speech” as “impolite” turns Paul’s boast into a confession of bad manners.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a narrowing, and it makes a plain verse unreadable. Rude in 1611 meant raw and unfinished, as an undressed stone is rude; today it means impolite, and nothing else. So the modern reader comes to “though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge” and hears an apostle apologizing for bad manners, when what Paul actually says is that he never trained in the orators’ guild and does not intend to. Corinth loved a polished performance; it had sized Paul up against the professionals and found his delivery contemptible. He concedes the point without a blush — grant the polish is absent — and then puts the knife in: yet not in knowledge. The world may keep its finish. He has the testimony of God.

The principle to recover is that God has never needed the guild. Paul did not stumble into plainness; he chose it: “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” — lest the cross of Christ be made of none effect, and lest the faith of his hearers stand in the wisdom of men rather than in the power of God. The council looked at Peter and John, perceived them unlearned and ignorant men, and marvelled — and then took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. That is the whole doctrine of the ministry in one verse. It is a standing rebuke to every age that measures a preacher by his polish, his stagecraft, his cleverness, or his platform, and it is a standing comfort to every plain man whom God has called: the pulpit’s power was never in the finish of the stone but in the Word that is quick and powerful and sharper than any two-edged sword.
roots_summary: The word means raw, unwrought, unpolished — unskilled in the orator’s art, not discourteous.
roots_lines: Rude — from Latin rudis, “raw, unwrought, rough.”
It is said of stone not yet dressed and timber not yet planed: unfinished.
The KJV sense is unpolished and untrained, not impolite; that meaning came later.
It renders the Greek idiōtēs, a layman without the guild’s training (2Co 11:6).
The same word marks Peter and John: unlearned men who had been with Jesus (Act 4:13).
usage: Though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge — Paul concedes the polish and keeps the truth.
Rude means unwrought, as an undressed stone is rude; it does not mean discourteous.
They perceived they were unlearned and ignorant men, and took knowledge that they had been with Jesus.
